utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we begin the cross-examination, or go on with it, rather, I would like to mention just some matters briefly about the calendar. There will be handed round a revised autumn calendar, necessary because one or two days we won't in fact be sitting, and also the plenary has been rearranged. So you'll get a copy of that, and I would remind you that it is of course necessarily a provisional calendar, and it will be subject to alteration because of other cases which the Trial Chamber has. The other matter concerns the final week of our sitting in this session, the week of the 2nd to the 6th of August. The 3rd of August, which is the Tuesday, we shall only be sitting in the morning. On Thursday, the 5th of August, we propose to hold a Status Conference. We think it's appropriate to consider the state of the case, to deal with any matters which the Defence or the accused may want to raise concerning their detention. We shall not be sitting on Friday, the 6th of August. Friday, the 6th of August, is off. So we shall finish with the Status Conference on the 5th. Very well. Yes, Mr. Surkovic, I'm sorry to hold your evidence up. We'll go on with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, my learned friends from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Surkovic. Allow me to continue with the examination by the Defence. You told us yesterday, Mr. Surkovic, that on the 16th of May, 1993, you were released, and that you left Vitez on that date. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you go from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went to Zenica, where my family was, and I joined my wife and sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you have been living in Zenica ever since then?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After those events in May 1993, have you had occasion to go back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Surkovic, how about your housing situation?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am a subtenant in Zenica, and I am paying 150 Deutschmarks rent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask the usher for his assistance, please, to show Mr. Surkovic yesterday's exhibit, Z2713.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In connection with this document, Mr. Surkovic, I have a few questions. First, will you tell me, if you know, where the document was written?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was written in Zenica. And if you know the town well, across the way from the former school of economics, or to be more precise, right next to the Premier Restaurant. That was where the Municipality of Vitez was housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the premises of Vitez municipality were in Zenica, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that was also where the authorities of Vitez municipality functioned?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you mean in exile? This went on for about one year, and then people returned to Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, do you know that while the authorities of Vitez municipality was functioning in Zenica, there was a -- parallel authorities were functioning in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. You mean Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I mean Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, sir, I have to point out that the town of Vitez is divided. A part of the town was controlled by the HVO, and the smaller part of the town, known as Stari Vitez, was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we had no contact with Stari Vitez, because we would have to cross territory controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Surkovic. But what I wanted to ask you about was whether you know that in the area controlled by the HVO, the Vitez municipality authority was operating.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you mean joint authority, no. Joint authorities are only just being established in the town of Vitez. In those days, it was only the HDZ authorities that were functioning in Kolonija, the greater part of Vitez, whereas in the old part of the town, there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that question. The authorities of Vitez municipality operating in Zenica, in terms of ethnic composition, which people was represented? Bosniaks and Croats, or only Bosniaks, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that must be clear to everyone. Only Bosniaks were represented in Zenica, and in Kolonija, in Vitez, only the Croats. And only now are joint authorities being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It follows from this document, Mr. Surkovic, that you were appointed, together with Mr. Dzidic, to a commission for caring for displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you please be kind enough to tell us very briefly, what was the main purpose of that commission?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I worked in Zenica for a year as a teacher. I know the town very well. And the refugees and displaced persons were mostly put up in schools. As I was familiar with these facilities, it was rather logical, and there were about 4.000 Bosniaks expelled from Vitez and put up in Zenica. It was normal that somebody who knew the town well and who would be capable of coordinating these activities, caring for the refugees. And that was the key reason why I was chosen, knowing the town rather well, and I think I coordinated those activities well. Also, we put up some families in the surrounding villages, in Janjici, Lokvine, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Surkovic, whether that commission of which you were a member, how was it financed? Did it have a budget, or did it collect funds, or did it have no funds?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If your question is whether we, as members of the commission, were paid for our work, we were not. In those days, there was hunger in Zenica. People were fighting for their bare existence. And occasionally we would get some foodstuffs, flour, potatoes, sugar, and this was mostly provided by humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Surkovic, you told us that you worked on the accommodation and care for displaced persons and refugees. Tell us, which ethnic groups did those people belong to?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I just said that about 4.000 Bosniaks were expelled from Vitez, and our task was to take care of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you engaged in these activities, caring for refugees and displaced persons, did you know that a certain number of Croats had also fled from Zenica to areas under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps have an idea of the figure of the people expelled from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, but I know that from certain villages, Croats left, and they went to the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a member of the commission, did you have any contact with Croats who had fled from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not have any contact with those people, because I don't know those people anyway. And another point that needs to be underlined, I didn't have any access to Vitez. And let me add that one displaced person from the surroundings of Vitez, during the fighting between the army and the HVO, was moved into my apartment, and so there was no possibility for me to enter Vitez in view of all those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to remove the exhibit on the ELMO and to replace it with an exhibit tendered by the Prosecution yesterday under the number Z2715.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, would you please explain to me what was the purpose of this document, this information signed by you and written by you as indicated on page 3, on the 8th of July, 1995? What is the purpose?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a brief report on camps in which Bosniaks from Vitez were detained. This is paragraph number 5. If necessary, I can go through the whole text. Another important thing is the number of houses destroyed and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Everyone can read what is in the document. My question is: Upon whose initiative or, rather, what were the motives that prompted you to write this report and in what capacity did you do so?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wrote this information to the state commission for the gathering of facts on war crimes in the territory of Vitez in this case, so that they know how many displaced persons there are, that they need to be aided in making a life for themselves again, that we know also how many buildings were destroyed, the condition of the housing fund, and the position of people displaced from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but I would like you to explain to me, did anyone officially ask you to provide these data that you did?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, I will answer your question but your question has nothing to do with my testimony yesterday. My duty as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, and I think it still is, to cooperate with bodies responsible for collecting facts on the crimes that occurred in the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that very difficult period of '92, '93, and '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. So as a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you felt it necessary to inform the competent state body of certain facts that you deposed of?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is my right as a citizen and I abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I should like to know what methodology you applied to obtain the data presented in this report. For example, how did you find out that in the second half of April 1993, about 5.000 citizens were expelled from the territory of Vitez municipality? Where did you get that figure from?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, in Zenica there was a committee for taking care of refugees and displaced persons. I point out it was not only Bosniaks that came to Zenica. There was a mass of refugees from Krajina, Kozarac, from Foca, Visegrad, and I'm underlining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you if I may. We'd like to finish your evidence, obviously. It would be helpful if you would just deal with the question as to where you got the information from in this report. Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just going to answer your questions. You're hurrying up, and I'm not sure I can answer properly because I have come to Zenica (sic) to tell the truth. I said that there were more than 40.000 refugees. There were files. There was a centre where information was collected on displaced persons and refugees. I coordinated the work of that centre, and I was able to collect exact figures but only for the territory of Vitez municipality regarding Bosniaks expelled from there who moved to Zenica, and I also had approximate figures for Travnik municipality. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you said that you obtained these figures from the records of the committee for displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Surkovic, will you please look at point 3 of your report? Please explain to me this allegation, but bear in mind that the report was written on the 8th of July, 1995. "On temporarily occupied territory of Vitez municipality," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It means the area controlled by the HVO. In that area, in the town of Vitez, according to data which are quite reliable, about 46 persons of Muslim nationality stayed behind. Why is this important? It is important, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter why it's important, if you'll forgive my saying so. Let us decide that. Mr. Mikulicic, this really isn't assisting us, you know, an argument about the phrasing of this particular paragraph. These sort of political points aren't going to assist us to try this case. By all means ask the witness where he got the information from. That is relevant. But a sterile political dispute isn't going to help us. Now, can we move on further in the document if you want to ask more about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, I must point out that the Defence doubts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, that was a ruling, not a matter for argument. Now, could you move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, according to the ruling of Their Honours, I should like to pass on to another document that was tendered yesterday. I'm talking of document Z2714.1, and I would like the usher to show it to you, please. Can you please tell us, very briefly, Mr. Surkovic, what kind of a document is it? What is it? I see here a number of photographs and some texts accompanying those photographs. Who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I compiled this part of the document. People who can read photographs and what is written under them will find it easy to assess the significance of this document and the message it carries. I wish to point out I have before me document 00473329, and it says "Zec Rasim, born in 1922." He was over 70 years old. He was a pensioner. The same applies to his wife. She was over 70. She was a housewife killed by a sniper on the 22nd of June, 1993. The purpose of the document is to show that civilians, and these were people in Stari Vitez, were killed for no reason at all by snipers. These were pensioners, over 70 years of age. Also, I have offered a document showing that a little boy of two was killed by a sniper. This can be confirmed by his mother. Another message carried by this document, the document 47331, it says Salih Tutso, his wife's name is unknown to me, a couple killed in their own home. The wife refused to move out though the children begged them to. HVO soldiers came and brutally murdered both of them in their house. So the message of this document too is the same. This happened in June 1993. The lines between the HVO and the army were stable, and these people were in the area under HVO control. There was absolutely no reason for innocent people who stayed in their own homes to be killed, murdered so brutally. The same applies to whole families, even those with five members. Your Honours, that was the purpose of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, the data contained in the document, the photographs, and the text, are they photographs that you yourself took?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "Yes" or "No,", please?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't take the late Salih Tutso, because he was already buried, but I was given this photograph by his sons. The same applies to other photographs. I was given them by members of their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. So you didn't take those photographs?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I just said that I received those photographs from their children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, are you the author of the text in this document written above and below the photographs?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where did you get the information for the text under the photographs? Let me be more specific what I'm particularly interested in. Document 00473316, the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you repeat?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the two mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you said that you were the author of the texts?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So tell me, the captions under the two photographs, it says, "My soldiers and I buried more than a hundred dead people." Does that mean that you were a military person, that you had your soldiers --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, sir. Please don't take it out of context. If you're really interested, this is a part of a document. Obviously I couldn't have taken the photograph of this demolished mosque. This was taken over from others. But as for the houses of Bosniaks, people, persons, they are mine. You happen to have selected these two mosques. I couldn't have taken those two pictures. I just copied down that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Surkovic, you spoke about this photograph with the Sehic couple, 00473329.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how do you know that this couple was killed by a sniper on the 22nd of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was told that by their son, who also gave me the photographs. This can easily be checked and verified. There are at least ten inhabitants of Stari Vitez who can confirm this, because those people were about to dig in their garden on the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Surkovic. My question was: Where did you get the facts from?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From their son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, talking to these people who gave you this information, did you take any notes about those conversations? Did you take statements from those people?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When it comes to these data or data of this kind, I took notes regarding date of birth, date of death. I compared the dates of birth and dates of death with the office -- with the relevant office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, can you tell us what the numbers written in by hand or typewritten indicate? For instance, there's the number "23" typewritten on the previous document. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are several pages. This was the numbering of the pages so that the order would not be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in concluding that the document you have here is not complete because pages 1 to 22 are missing?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course not. This is only a part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I asked you earlier what your methodology was to determine the facts, so I will ask you again. The facts that you discovered in this way, did you check them additionally?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, I never accept any facts as ready facts. I always check them from several sources. I claim that this is all correct. It's well documented and argued. It can be proved with the help of witnesses. A lot of people from Stari Vitez could confirm this. There are a lot of people who confirm what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Surkovic, that after the 16th of May, 1993, you never went to that region?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the 16th of May, 1993? Sir, I have to correct you this time. Before I came here, perhaps, I went to the high school in Kruscica. I worked there. I passed through Vitez. The situation was much better than it used to be. I walked through Kolonija, where I couldn't even go before. It's true that I can go there any time that I want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Surkovic, when you say that you can go to that territory, did you make any kind of additional checking of those facts?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The facts that are stated here are checked. Even certain data has been checked through the Office of the Registrar. There are a lot of people who are familiar with the situation, and I claim that these are facts which have been checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Surkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, let me understand this: Is it disputed that there were 95 people killed in Ahmici, for instance? You see, what I'm wondering is how much of this evidence is really in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is being contested by the Defence is the accuracy of the data in documents 2714 and 2715, because we believe that the witness is not qualified to carry out these kind of investigations, and we believe that the applied methodology in working on these documents does not meet the criteria that it should. So that is why the Defence doubts the accuracy of these documents, and the Defence is opposed to having these documents entered into exhibits. The witness discussed about these facts that he knew through personal -- that he saw personally, but he is not an expert; he is not capable of providing studies or expertise or any kind of similar work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His evidence is that he collected them. Whether he is an expert or not, this is information which he collected, one way and another. What I'm asking you is, whether the figure is 95 or whatever, is it disputed that a very large number of people were killed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, that is not contested, Your Honour, whether it's 95, 108, or 93. The witness doesn't know that. The Defence doesn't know that. But what is contested is that the methodology that these documents were done in are in contrary with the Latin saying "auditur et altera pas." The witness determined these facts exclusively by discussing one side in the conflict, and this is what we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stein, have you got any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not over the same ground again, as far as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, if there is any question that I ask you that you don't understand, will you let me know?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I represent Dario Kordic. My name is Bob Stein. If you could, sir, when I ask you a question that's capable of being answered "Yes" or "No," we would all appreciate if you answered "Yes" or "No." Is that all right? Now, the other thing I have to tell you, you have to answer so the reporters hear you, which means you have to say "Yes," "No," whatever your answer is, into the microphone. Is that all right? In other words, you can't just nod your head. Okay. Let me ask you first, sir, when Aleksovski, upon your release, announced that the exchange was delayed and then half an hour later told you that Kordic had ordered the exchange to go forward, you did not believe that Kordic had ordered that exchange; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, you thought that was a way to try to increase the authority of Dario Kordic in the eyes of your fellow prisoners; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned earlier in your testimony yesterday that you have a diary, you've been keeping a diary?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that's a diary you kept before the war, during the war, and even up to today?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you use that diary to look at to refresh your recollection before you testified today?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, it's not my diary. My diary is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Whose diary is it?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you share that diary with members of the Office of the Prosecutor, the investigators, or their staff? Did you show it to them?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, I do not want to do that. It's a personal, private matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, you appeared in Zenica in October of 1993, before a tribunal there. Before that appearance, did you discuss your testimony with Edib Zlotrg?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Afterwards, did you discuss --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At any time, did you discuss your testimony or your appearance before the tribunal in Zenica with Mr. Zlotrg?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In March, Mr. Zlotrg was here with me, Your Honours. We were together in the same hotel. He testified and I testified, so we went to dinner every evening, and we went to lunch together every day. But it's not a habit after the proceedings to talk about all of these things which are pretty exhausting for us and which we really can't wait to forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So you're telling the Tribunal that neither you nor Mr. Zlotrg shared information over these dinners?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not talk with him. I was very clear, we would talk about sports, our families. There was no need to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to turn to your background a bit. You are indeed a professional politician; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I am a teacher. I'm a professor at high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me change the tense: You were a professional politician at one point in time. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And indeed, you were employed as president of the Committee of the League of Communists for one year; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that's a paid position?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you were employed for one year as a director of a private company in Vitez, the Our company, O-U-R?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was not a private company. It was an engine construction factory, one of the Unis complex factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And your position there was organiser of the labour, or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I was the director of that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That, too, was a paid position?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that was a political position; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. I was a businessman. I organised the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, despite those two years, the majority of your work has been teaching; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And at one point you even became principal of a high school?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Most of your teaching, if not all, and your principal of the high school, was done under the communist regime?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You didn't teach physics --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: However, I still teach at the high school, and I'm a mechanical engineer. So I teach expert scientific subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But you don't teach physics, I hope? Never mind; I was just trying to make a point that I don't want to make any more. My point is, sir, that you were in fact the principal of a high school under the communist system, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I do not teach physics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. You were a principal of a high school under the communist system?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you were aware of the curriculum for that school?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that curriculum was given to you by the central government; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The federal ministry of education, that would be the body that would determine the curriculum. The school system was centralised then. We're now decentralising the educational system. The educational system is organised by cantons now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. And the central federal ministry of education were the ones that determined which books the students would read; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The federal ministry would order -- commission new textbooks. The textbooks that are satisfactory, that are accepted, would be applied. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: After the war, actually during the war and after the war, all that changed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, before the war, under the communist regime, in the schools, the doctrine of brotherhood and unity was taught; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And any kind of dissent about ethnic relations, religions, was frowned upon and punished; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You can neither confirm nor deny that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were no cases of deviation from the prescribed curriculum. As far as inter-ethnic relations are concerned, in my community, in Vitez, there were no disagreements between Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. People lived in tolerance, they lived together in harmony, and it was good for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That, in fact, was what the communist system demanded: True, or not true?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These were norms of civilised behaviour, and this is how we all behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that was also a norm of the communist system that made you behave that way: True, or not true?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was no anarchy. We all worked, and we all had a good living. I cannot blame the communist system for what happened afterwards: that we fought, that we bled, that we destroyed our homes. I think that the blame lies in another source and not in the communist system. You are stressing, emphasising the communist system, and I don't understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll only ask this one more time. It's very clear. Under the communist system, it was required that everyone, according to the communist system rules which did not allow for the kind of dissent, the kind of criticism of ethnic relations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, you've asked that question a number of times. I'm not sure I see what the relevance of the communist system to the present case is. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: You did indicate under the communist system you weren't a practising Muslim, but now you are, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, the faith and my religious orientation are my private matter. So I would ask you not to delve into my private matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it, sir, that it was certainly easier to practice your religion now than it was under either regime, and as a professional politician it became easier for you to practice religion now under the old regime?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not a professional politician now, and I'm not sure how professional politicians feel now. In any case, I know that they have a hard time because the country's destroyed. The people have quarrelled. The country's destroyed. So it's probably much more difficult for them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's me turn to the first elections under the new regime. The Croats in your area were a majority, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were about 4 per cent more Croats than Muslims. If you're interested, there was about 41.7 per cent Muslims, 45 per cent for Croats, and Serbs 5.4 per cent. This was from the census in '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In the parliament, the HDZ held a majority as well, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It had 23 deputies. The SDA had 16. The left block, the SDP, the Liberals and the Reformists had 19. I was a member of the parliament, so that's how I know this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So the score was 23 -- or the ratio, rather, was 23 to 19; right?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The ratio, as far as HDZ and the left oriented block, the SDP, the Liberals and the reform forces are concerned, but the SDA had 16 deputies in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If you add the 16 deputies and the Liberal wing on other hand and on the other hand the HDZ, it's 23 to 19.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how you're adding it up. I don't know what the "23" refers to. I know that the HDZ had 23 representatives, but the SDA and the HDZ got on quite well together, but later on they quarrelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Were you a member of the crisis committee that formed during the war?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm aware of the functions of the crisis staff but I was not a member. The crisis staff was formed so that the nationalist passions which had started awaken among the people would calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you anything about -- I asked if you were a member and your answer's "No."

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I have a statement here from Dr. Mujenznovic. On page 4, statement given to this Tribunal, in which he says: "Enes Surkovic, who was a member of the crisis committee that I presided over, was assigned to keep track of a number of the Muslims who lost their homes and were dispossessed." I take it you disagree with his representation?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not true. May I explain? But it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: At the end of 1992, there was a coordination committee which had been disbanded and a war committee was formed. You were part of that war committee, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. And that war committee was sometimes called the Coordinating Committee for the Protection of Muslims, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Was that a different group, the Coordinating Committee for the Protection of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was a different body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just want to let the Court know. We do not have the document in front us that is being referred to. So if there is a possibility of a copy, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I actually wasn't referring to anything, but my next thing is relative to D13/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You knew people on the Coordinating Committee for the Protection of Muslims, correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujenznovic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We're good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. And because of that friendship with Dr. Mujenznovic and other individuals, you're aware that the committee for the protection of Muslims was entrusted with the task of setting up the barricade in October of 1992, October 19 and 20, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How does this arise from his examination-in-chief, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He mentioned the barricade, I believe. If he didn't, I'll stand corrected and I'll withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that. We were, in fact, going fairly rapidly through his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you straightaway, sir, after the crisis committee, which was a group coordinating the war against the Serbs, diminished, and certainly as you explained to my colleague, there were actually parallel governments in Vitez and the environment, Muslims and Croats, correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When the Muslims moved to Stari Vitez, and this happened about November 25th in 1992, it could be said that two governments functioned. They were both weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good. I want to point out that in those two governments there was a person in charge in your government and in the Muslim government of finance, a person in charge of education, a person in charge of police, a person in charge of logistics, and other kinds of things; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed there was a declaration adopted about that time that the Muslims of Vitez do not recognise the newly established one-nation government in Vitez, and the HVO government and all of its decisions were not to be binding on Muslims, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't in the political circles at that time but I think, yes, that that claim is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, I want to talk to you about a period after October of 1992. It's fair to say that the Muslims who had telescopic -- I'm sorry, the Muslims who had hunting rifles with telescopes on them became the object of the Croats' seizures, which is a terrible question, so let me try again. The Croats took any Muslim who had a hunting rifle with a scope on it, that rifle from him; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but I don't claim that they confiscated them from everybody. They could not have done that because they probably didn't know about all the people who had the weapons, but they did confiscate them, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So there were some hunting rifles with telescopic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There were some --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if the hunting rifles had the telescopic sights, but I know that people did have hunting rifles. There were a lot of hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we also agree that before April 16, 1993, that you believed that the war was inevitable?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I had believed that war was inevitable, I would have moved my wife and children from Vitez and I would have moved to a safer place. I would not have spent that time in the camps under very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm looking at a translation that was given to me yesterday, and on page 10 of the English of that translation, you're quoted as -- and by the way, to be fair with you, this is a copy of your appearance before Judge Safet Adrovic in Zenica. You appeared in front of that judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm a good friend of Safet Adrovic, and I never gave him a statement, but I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You appeared in front of him in the court in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never appeared in court or before him, but I did often go and have coffee with him and we would sit together, but I never went to see Safet to make any kind of personal statement. I have no need of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You did not appear in front of a court clerk named Sadika Mujezinovic and a public prosecutor named Sauda Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Adrovic is employed at the prosecutor's office, and I know that he's in charge and I saw him on television. He's in charge of investigating mass graves. But as far as gathering evidence or statements from witnesses, I don't remember ever giving him a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were born in 1944, were you not? Unless we have a stipulation, I'm going to go through all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you're not. Now, what's the position of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask if perhaps the witness were shown the B/C/S version of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let him see the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This was a document provided in B/C/S. It was the subject of the translation issue yesterday. I think it would be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got a copy to show the witness, in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll be happy to hand my copy over. Yes, Mr. Usher -- whatever. This is the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't point to the page, but let me suggest in the English, sir -- take a look at the last page. Take a look at the very last page, sir.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just see the date, please. I really do know Safet Adrovic very well, but I do not remember at all giving such a statement to Mr. Adrovic. However, I see the initials of my signature here in 1994. This was in 1994. I really cannot remember such a document, though I do know Mr. Adrovic very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I know you can't remember appearing in that proceeding, but the Office of the Prosecutor has supplied us with that record of that proceeding, and page 10 of the English version to, get to what I was saying, you were quoted as saying: "It was obvious that war between the BH army and the HVO in this area was inevitable." Now, I can't find the parallel citation yet in Croatian, but Mr. Naumovski will do that shortly.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try again. Have you looked over that document?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked through it. There's no need for me to read it. It's a very lengthy document. There are lots of signatures here. I know Mr. Adrovic very well. Since this document is here and my signature it's probably true, but I do not recall making a statement in court to Mr. Adrovic ever, but my signature is there in '94. Now it is '99, but probably it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to do it easily, I ask Your Honours to take a look at the statement at page 10, the English translation. The first full paragraph: "It was obvious that war between the BH army and the HVO in this area was inevitable." " It's at page 5 of the Croatian, about mid-page. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, beyond his memory, can he confirm or deny this phrase to which you appear to attach importance? So ask him the question, please. What does he think about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough, Judge. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Having read you your testimony, and indeed if you want to look at page 5, middle of the page, you'll find it quoted there, page 5 --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you remember, first, saying that to the judge, that's the first part, and if you do or don't it doesn't matter, does that at least refresh your mind as to how in 1993 you felt about the war, that is, that it was inevitable?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 15th of April, 1993, on that date I attended a meeting in the fire brigade centre. We were celebrating army day. Mr. Cerkez was present too. The civilian authorities of Vitez municipality were claiming that there would be no war and that agreement had been reached with the other side to ease tensions. However, the average citizen, on the eve of the war, realises that something was wrong, that tensions were running high, that the situation was abnormal in town. On the 15th of April, if I could have taken my wife and children from Vitez, I would have, but I wasn't sure of our safety on the road so I had to stay where I was. Therefore, on the eve of the conflict, it was clear to citizens that the conflict would break out, but months before that the situation was much better, and no one expected such a bloody settling of accounts nor so many murders. A bloody showdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to Kaonik, very briefly. While you were in Kaonik, there were also 10 to 12 Arabs also imprisoned; yes?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: These Arabs were Arab soldiers, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. They were people in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Who were they, where did they come from, and why were they there?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me too much. I was a detainee too. I didn't have supper even with people I had shared the cell with, never mind these people. I saw them cleaning the compound when I was going to see a doctor at the health centre in Busovaca. I also heard screams at night from the cell where the Arabs were held, and not just me, but all those who were with me, but they were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you this: You indicated earlier that your release was ordered by a man named Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Petkovic is a military man; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, April 30th, some week or two before your release, there was another military officer who visited you in Kaonik and that was General Halilovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's fair, is it not, to say that General Halilovic and General Petkovic negotiated for your release?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So two military officers negotiated for the release of the prisoners from Kaonik; fair? Agreed?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My wife and some friends told me that Mr. Sefer Halilovic and Mr. Milivoj Petkovic had spoken on television late in the evening, sometime around the 10th of May. They had a fierce debate regarding the situation on the ground and regarding detainees, and I was told that Sefer Halilovic requested for Milivoj Petkovic to explain where the 13 men taken from Vitez were. These were mostly people with university degrees that used to hold political office. She told me that the debate was very passionate, and I personally spoke to Sefer Halilovic in the cinema hall. I don't know what part of that conversation may be of interest to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The short answer to my question, sir, is yes, two military offices negotiated for the release of those 13 prisoners; yes?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. And they negotiated about the involvement of joint forces in the struggle against the former JNA and the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were released in exchange for the release of other soldiers; correct? Strike that. You were released in exchange --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were released in exchange for other civilians, like yourself, Croat civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Croat civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. How many Croat civilians were released at the same time you were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And were there any -- strike that; I'll rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm almost at the end of my examination, for the Court's edification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: The term "Bosniak," that was a term that was not used before 1992; isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not true. It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The term "Bosniak" was not used under the communist regime, was it?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You will find the term in medieval literature. It implied an inhabitant of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "A good old Bosniak" is the expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As a common term to describe the Muslim people, before 1992, that term was not used; agreed?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's "Yes" or "No." You either agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The unresolved national question in the former Yugoslavia was a stumbling block. No, that term "Bosniak" was not used, but instead a Muslim with a capital "M." And the difference between Muslims with a capital and with a small "m" is considerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. And now, of course, the term "Bosniak" is used to represent the term for the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A Bosujanin is an inhabitant of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but a Bosujanin of Muslim faith is a Muslim of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because there are Bosniaks among Croats and Serbs of orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Even better for my purposes, sir. Now, my last question to you is this: Before the war, the elementary school in Vitez was called "The School of Brotherhood and Unity"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you know what it's called now?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The elementary school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yeah. That's what it's called? The elementary school in Vitez? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked about the conditions in the first place of detention where you were taken, which was the basement of your apartment building, and you specifically indicated that -- the question was whether or not it was suitable for people to take refuge. Was the basement of the Radnicki Univerzitet suitable for people to be kept?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The answer is no. It was the former boiler room of the Workers' University, where they kept coal and ashes from the furnace.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The cinema, to which we were moved around the 20th -- some earlier on -- was much better before the bomb truck exploded on the 18th of April. As a result of that explosion, the glass broke, so that it was cold in the cinema, and we didn't have any blankets or any other covers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But in the Radnicki Univerzitet, had you observed signs of construction that might have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Probably more as clarification. My dear colleague, Ms. Somers, in the first question, implied that the witness yesterday said that he was taken to the basement of the apartment building, which wasn't really the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it was where he, himself, went to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but he was not taken there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It implies that he was --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any sign of construction in the Radnicki Univerzitet that you noticed, that caught your attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's certainly beyond the scope of cross on both of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Do you think that's going to help us any more? We've heard evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Judge, if I could comment: Yesterday, because we did go from question 7 to question 25, there was a point that was touched upon about some construction that suggested -- I think, if the witness does recall, I would have liked to have gone -- but I'm afraid that I want to tag it on now because I think the question of construction suitability for people being packed together is relevant, and it's the only issue on terms of confinement that I would address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can do so, but briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you notice any signs of recent construction -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Can I answer that question? Yes, I do remember that when we were brought there, we noticed that water, a tap had been installed, and to judge by the fresh mortar, we assessed that it had been done a couple of days before. Also electrical installation work had been done. Again, we could judge this by the plaster on the wall, that it had been freshly done, so that obviously this room was being prepared for people to live in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The issue of your being a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina was raised. Were there persons in the Vitez area who displayed loyalty to republics or other sovereigns beside Bosnia and Herzegovina during the time frame that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please be a little clearer? Which other States are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there people who were expressing loyalty to the Republic of Croatia, or to a Croatian entity, or to an entity other than Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is the tragedy of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some people are loyal to Zagreb; others support Belgrade; a third want to have an integral and unified Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is a fact, and that is what has led to certain disagreements and consequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The separate parallel governments referred to by counsel that arose in November of 1992 were Muslim or Bosniak and Croat governments. However, was there not a separate, parallel set of institutions for education, for banking, for infrastructure, set in place when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded one year earlier, in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, teaching in the secondary school centre was organised throughout that time, until the 16th of April, 1993, for all pupils of Croat, Serb, and Bosniak ethnicity, or rather Muslim or Islamic faith. But already then, after the 20th of October, 1992, and I underline that was the time of the first conflict between the HVO and the BH army, tensions were running high even among teachers and also among pupils. Unfortunately, the situation on the ground was being transposed upon our children as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Forgive me; perhaps I wasn't quite clear enough. Were there not institutions, such as educational and financial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there is any dispute about this, is there? Is there any dispute about this? We've heard a lot of evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you were not the only political person to have taught high school in Vitez; is that correct? Anto Valenta also taught high school in Vitez, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Valenta and Mr. Kajmovic Munir (phoen) worked with me in Vitez. Mr. Valenta was a member of the leadership of the HDZ, and Mr. Kajmovic was president of the SDA party, and frequently there were polemics and disagreements among people, and this was felt by the children, of course. If you wish, I can describe an unfortunate incident that occurred in the secondary school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You've answered that question. One additional point on that would be on the slogan of brotherhood and unity that counsel mentioned to you. Would you describe, based on what you know about Anto Valenta, as Mr. Valenta being an advocate of brotherhood and unity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to allow that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, one quick question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The circumstances surrounding your release, the order that was issued under the direction of General Petkovic, you indicated the enforcement of that order was delayed for some 20 minutes or half an hour, according to Mr. Aleksovski. Was it or was it not your understanding that it was Dario Kordic, or the word or authority of Dario Kordic, that overrode that delay of an order --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's absolutely leading and not appropriate in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I haven't stopped you before. We are not in the courts of the United States. We are not accustomed to constant interruption here. Now, it may well be that there is a leading element in the question, and to that extent, the answer becomes worthless. We are accustomed to dealing with such matters, so will you leave it in our hands. Ms. Somers, you heard that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Shall I rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's much point; do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are no further questions, Your Honour, no further redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, thank you very much for coming to give evidence to the International Tribunal. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's coming up to the time for a break, but are there any applications before the next witness gives evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are. Your Honour, if we could go into private session for the purposes of not disclosing the name of the next witness at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 5.40 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of July, 1999 at 2:30 p.m.
